tier_reason: Independent third-party measurement: OneFlow's DLPerf report v1.0 runs MXNet, TensorFlow and PyTorch from public per-framework scripts (Oneflow-Inc/DLPerf MxNet/, TensorFlow/, PyTorch/, NVIDIADeepLearningExamples/) on stated hardware (Xeon Gold 5118, 4x8 V100-SXM2-16GB); prebuilt containers and wheels with no compiler or flags, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: ResNet-50 v1.5 FP32 bsz 128, 1 GPU: upstream MXNet 1.6.0 (gluon-cv) 384.19 img/s vs PyTorch 1.6.0 348.62 and TensorFlow 2.3 321.80 (1.10x and 1.19x, derived from page data); NVIDIA NGC MXNet 392.24 vs NGC PyTorch 367.29 and NGC TensorFlow 1.15 362.44. 32 GPUs FP32: NGC MXNet 11331.93 vs NGC PyTorch 10917.09 (1.04x) and NGC TensorFlow 1.x 9514.64 (1.19x), derived from page data; upstream MXNet 9579.74 is behind PyTorch 10021.29 and only 1.02x over TensorFlow 2.3 9418.44. AMP bsz 256, 32 GPUs: NGC MXNet 30713.68 vs NGC TensorFlow 1.x with XLA 29171.69 and NGC PyTorch 22551.16, but upstream MXNet 10565.55 is far behind TensorFlow 2.3 19314.31. BERT-base FP32 bsz max, 32 GPUs: MXNet without clip_by_global_norm (bsz 64) 4340.89 sentences/s vs NGC TensorFlow 1.x 3089.74 and NGC PyTorch 3039.3 (both bsz 48, with gradient clipping); the TensorFlow 2.3 figure 2244.38 (bsz 64) is in the DLPerf README summary table, not in the report.
corrections.caveats: The benchmark is run by OneFlow, a competing framework, from public scripts in Oneflow-Inc/DLPerf; OneFlow beats MXNet in every row quoted. All frameworks call cuDNN and cuBLAS for the convolutions and GEMMs, so the gaps measure framework overhead, input pipelines (NGC rows use DALI) and distributed communication, not kernels. The MXNet margin is small and not consistent: upstream MXNet 1.6.0 gluon-cv is slower than PyTorch 1.6.0 on 8 GPUs (2556.03 vs 2632.93 img/s) and on 32 GPUs (9579.74 vs 10021.29), and beats TensorFlow 2.3 by only 1.02x there (9418.44). With AMP, upstream MXNet is roughly half the speed of TensorFlow 2.3 and NGC PyTorch (10565.55 vs 19314.31 and 22551.16 img/s on 32 GPUs; 2908.88 vs 6898.00 on 8 GPUs). The large NGC MXNet figures come from NVIDIA's tuned DeepLearningExamples container with DALI and Horovod, not upstream MXNet. The BERT rows are not like-for-like: MXNet's gluon-nlp script has no clip_by_global_norm, which the report says raises throughput and may lower accuracy, and it ran at bsz 64 against bsz 48 for the NGC baselines; OneFlow run the same way (W/O clip) is faster than MXNet. The DLPerf README summary shows NGC MXNet 32-GPU FP32 as 11233.92 while the report shows 11331.93. Versions are from 2020 (TensorFlow 2.3, PyTorch 1.6), so current TensorFlow and PyTorch 2.x numbers have moved. An older NeurIPS 2019 PyTorch paper table (MXNet 218, PyTorch 212, TensorFlow 200 img/s, seen only as a search snippet; arXiv and NeurIPS blocked) points the same way. The repository was renamed apache/mxnet and archived (read-only) on 2023-11-17; Apache MXNet was retired to the Attic.

notes: Numbers verified on the report; last commit 2023-01-26 confirmed from the master commit feed, 20.8k stars, Apache-2.0; TensorFlow 2.x BERT 2244.38 exists only in the DLPerf README, and the BERT comparison mixes an unclipped optimizer and larger batch for MXNet. Shortcomings for the orchestrator: framework-level benchmark run by a competitor, cuDNN under every framework, MXNet wins only at 1 GPU upstream or with NVIDIA's NGC container, upstream MXNet loses badly with AMP, project archived. repo_url apache/incubator-mxnet redirects to apache/mxnet (consider a repo_url override); TensorFlow and PyTorch are not in the autodiff-and-ml-kernels baseline list, so baseline_in_list is false.

tier_reason: Independent community measurement with public harness code (u39kun/deep-learning-benchmark benchmark.py, frameworks/pytorch/models.py, frameworks/tensorflow/models.py) and stated GPUs, CUDA and cuDNN versions; prebuilt NGC images, no host CPU model and no build flags, so not A. Corroborated by the independent DLPerf v1.0 report.

corrections.caveats: The benchmark is a small community repo (u39kun, not project-authored) with 2017-2019 framework versions (PyTorch 0.3.0 and 1.0.0 against TensorFlow 1.4 to 1.12 graph mode), so it says little about TensorFlow 2.x with XLA or PyTorch 2.x. Both frameworks call cuDNN for the convolutions, so the gaps measure framework overhead and kernel selection, not new kernels. The harness is not symmetric: the TensorFlow training step fetches every gradient tensor back to the host through sess.run(self.grad) (a device-to-host copy the PyTorch loop does not do) and builds the graph with phase_train=False, while the PyTorch loop also computes a gradient for the input image (requires_grad=True) and enables cudnn.benchmark autotuning; the size of these effects was not measured. The win is mixed: TensorFlow 1.12 is faster on vgg16 training on the 2080 Ti (90.8 vs 95.5 ms FP32, 58.6 vs 68.1 ms FP16); on the V100, TensorFlow 1.5.0 beats PyTorch 0.3.0 on vgg16 (eval 24.0 vs 26.2 ms, train 71.7 vs 83.5 ms) while PyTorch wins resnet152 train (136.5 vs 199.8 ms); on the 1080 Ti vgg16 train is 131.3 (TensorFlow) vs 131.9 ms; eval times are mostly within about 4% (Titan V FP32 vgg16 eval 31.3 vs 31.8 ms). Results are batch size 16 only, synthetic inputs, 20 timed iterations after 20 warm-ups. A second independent source, Oneflow-Inc/DLPerf report v1.0 (Oct 2020, 4x8 V100 GPUs, ResNet-50 v1.5 FP32, bsz 128), has PyTorch 1.6.0 10021.29 img/s vs TensorFlow 2.3 9418.44 (1.06x, derived from page data) and NGC PyTorch 10917.09 vs NGC TensorFlow 1.x 9514.64, but with AMP NGC PyTorch 22551.16 loses to NGC TensorFlow 1.x both with XLA (29171.69) and without (24734.22), and on BERT-base NGC TensorFlow wins the FP32 bsz-max row (3089.74 vs 3039.3) and the AMP bsz-64 row with XLA (9409.2 vs 9331.72); that report was read at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Oneflow-Inc/DLPerf/HEAD/reports/dlperf_benchmark_test_report_v1.md. The PyTorch NeurIPS 2019 paper table (MXNet 218, PyTorch 212, TensorFlow 200 img/s ResNet-50, seen only as a search snippet) was not readable because arXiv and NeurIPS are blocked.

notes: All claimed numbers match the u39kun README. Metadata checked: BSD-3-Clause, 103.8k stars, last commit 2026-10-07; the u39kun repo has 427 stars and no license. Shortcomings for the orchestrator: old framework versions, mixed results (TensorFlow wins vgg16 train on 2080 Ti and V100, and AMP ResNet-50 in DLPerf), asymmetric harness (TensorFlow train fetches gradients to host, BN in inference mode), cuDNN under both frameworks. TensorFlow is not in the autodiff-and-ml-kernels baseline list, so baseline_in_list is false.

tier_reason: The TensorFlow RFC only quotes 'up to' speedups from Intel and TensorFlow blog posts (Intel Medium, blog.tensorflow.org, intel.com), with no models, batch sizes, CPU SKUs, versions or harness on the page; vendor numbers without methodology are C.

corrections.caveats: Vendor claim: the RFC (TensorFlow community RFC #400, author Penporn Koanantakool of Google, sponsor Tatiana Shpeisman) quotes Intel's own numbers from Intel Medium, blog.tensorflow.org and intel.com posts that were blocked here, so only the RFC's summary was read; model list, batch sizes, TensorFlow version, CPU SKUs and flags are not given on the page. 'Up to' figures are best cases, and the RFC itself says oneDNN ops can be slower than standard TensorFlow CPU ops in rare cases because of primitive preparation and graph-rewrite overhead. Part of the gain is instruction-set dispatch: default TensorFlow packages were built for AVX only, and since TF 1.13 the default Eigen contraction path already calls oneDNN's single-threaded dnnl_sgemm in place of Eigen's gebp kernel, so the 'default Eigen ops' baseline already contains oneDNN code for matmul and convolution. TensorFlow has since turned oneDNN ops on by default in x86 Linux builds (from 2.9 per Intel's guide, search snippet only), so the baseline exists only with TF_ENABLE_ONEDNN_OPTS=0. No head-to-head against OpenBLAS or MKL was found: the issue #415 search hit has no numbers, and a search for independent oneDNN-vs-Eigen measurements returned only Intel pages. oneDNN is itself a listed baseline (incumbent) of the autodiff-and-ml-kernels category. The project is now governed by the UXL Foundation; github.com/oneapi-src/oneDNN redirects to github.com/uxlfoundation/oneDNN.

notes: Metadata checked: Apache-2.0, 4.1k stars, last commit 2026-10-07. RFC numbers match (3x inference, 2.4x training on Cascade Lake; 1.7-1.9x more with bfloat16 on Cooper Lake; 3-4x int8 on Cascade Lake), but they are Intel's own; the RFC author is from Google, not Intel. oneDNN is the named incumbent of autodiff-and-ml-kernels in spec Part 4, so the orchestrator may treat it as a category incumbent (duplicate precedent for boostorg/geometry, flame/blis, SuiteSparse); the id's canonical home is now uxlfoundation/oneDNN.
